# Diversity and differential abundance over time {#sec-time-diversity}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

chapterPreamble()
```

```{r}

#| include: false

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    message = FALSE,
    fig.width = 10,
    dpi = 300,
    dev = "png",
    dev.args = list(type = "cairo-png")

```

Alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance analyses from the
previous chapters can be applied to longitudinal data. The difference is that
samples from the same subject are paired, and the analysis has to take this
into account.

In this chapter, we use an example dataset from a probiotic/placebo
intervention study. The dataset includes gut microbiota samples from 22
subjects and 2 time points. The first time point was sampled before
introducing a treatment.

```{r}
#| label: load_data

library(mia)
library(microbiomeDataSets)

mae <- peerj32()
tse <- getWithColData(mae, 1L)
tse[["time_point"]] <- tse[["time"]] |> as.factor()
```

## Alpha diversity

[@sec-alpha-diversity] introduced alpha diversity. Here we calculate the
Shannon index and visualize it by time point. Lines connect the samples of each
subject.

```{r}
#| label: alpha_plot

library(miaViz)

tse <- addAlpha(tse, index = "shannon")

plotBoxplot(
    tse,
    col.var = "shannon",
    x = "time_point",
    pair.by = "subject",
    colour.by = "group",
    facet.by = "group"
)
```

The plot does not show a clear change in either group. Because the samples are
paired, we use the paired Wilcoxon test separately for each group.

```{r}
#| label: alpha_wilcoxon

df <- colData(tse) |> as.data.frame()
df <- df[order(df[["subject"]]), ]

lapply(split(df, df[["group"]]), function(x) {
    wilcox.test(
        x[x[["time_point"]] == 1, "shannon"],
        x[x[["time_point"]] == 2, "shannon"],
        paired = TRUE
    )
})
```

Neither group shows a significant change in Shannon diversity between the
time points. The tests above do not compare the groups. A linear mixed model
can test whether the change over time differs between the groups. The
`time * group` term includes the effects of time and group and their
interaction, and `(1 | subject)` adds a random effect for each subject to
account for the repeated measurements.

```{r}
#| label: alpha_lmm

library(lmerTest)

model <- lmer(shannon ~ time * group + (1 | subject), data = df)
summary(model)
```

The interaction term "time:groupPlacebo" tests whether the change in Shannon
diversity from the first to the second time point differs between the Placebo
and LGG groups. The interaction is not significant, so the change in diversity
does not differ between the groups.

## Beta diversity

[@sec-community-similarity] introduced ordination. In longitudinal data, we
can connect the samples of each subject in the ordination plot to show how the
communities changed over time.

```{r}
#| label: beta_ordination

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")
tse <- addMDS(tse, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray")

plotOrdination(
    tse,
    dimred = "MDS",
    colour.by = "group",
    pair.by = "subject",
    sort.by = "time"
)
```

The arrows show no consistent shift that would separate the groups.

The change can also be quantified as the dissimilarity between consecutive
samples of the same subject, i.e., divergence (see [@sec-divergence]).

```{r}
#| label: beta_divergence

library(miaTime)

tse <- addStepwiseDivergence(
    tse,
    time.col = "time",
    group = "subject",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray"
)

# Divergence is calculated for the second time point
plotBoxplot(
    tse[, tse[["time_point"]] == 2],
    col.var = "divergence",
    x = "group"
)
```

Divergence between the time points is similar in both groups.

## Differential abundance

[@sec-differential-abundance] introduced differential abundance analysis. With
paired samples, the subject has to be included in the model. Below, we use
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("LimROTS")` [@Anwar2025] to test which taxa changed
between the time points in the LGG group. The argument `correlation_block`
specifies the subject, so that samples from the same subject are resampled
together and their correlation is accounted for in the model. LimROTS requires
log-transformed data, so we use the CLR transformation.

```{r}
#| label: daa_limrots

library(LimROTS)

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "clr", pseudocount = TRUE)
tse_lgg <- tse[, tse[["group"]] == "LGG"]

set.seed(123)
tse_lgg <- LimROTS(
    tse_lgg,
    assay.type = "clr",
    niter = 200,
    meta.info = c("time_point", "subject"),
    group = "time_point",
    formula.str = "~ 0 + time_point",
    correlation_block = "subject",
    BPPARAM = BiocParallel::SerialParam(),
    verbose = FALSE
)

res <- rowData(tse_lgg)[, c("corrected.logfc", "pvalue", "qvalue")]
res[order(res[["pvalue"]]), ] |> head()
```

`corrected.logfc` is the first time point minus the second, so negative values
mean higher abundance at the second time point. In the LGG group,
*Lactobacillus plantarum et rel.* increased after the intervention.

LimROTS compares the levels of one categorical variable. To test whether the
change differs between the groups, use a model with an interaction term as in
the alpha diversity example above.
